To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

substance P (SP), and/or its close relative, neurokinin A, prolong thermal stimulus-evoken responses in wide dynamic range (WDR) neurons in the dorsal horn of the lumbar spinal cord in preprota-chykinin-A (-/-) mutant mice, and that SP and/or neurokinin A are not required for the intensity coding or sensitizing actions of WDR neurons in the dorsal spinal cord.

substance P and neurokinin-A are not required for nociceptive transmission, but that their absence reduces the magnitude and duration (i.e., the intensity and duration of the behavioral response) of the nocifensive response to intense stimuli.
the deletion of the ppt-A gene, from which the neuropeptides substance P and neurokinin-A are derived, does not affect the coding of noxious thermal stimuli in the spinal cord of mice in vivo.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role that substance P and neurokinin receptors play in the spinal cord in the processing of noxious information and pain.
understanding how sensory neurons in the spinal dorsal horn process and encode noxious stimuli, and the role of neuropeptides in this process.
elucidating the mechanisms of nociception and pain, with a particular emphasis on the role of peptides in nociceptive transmission and the development of hypersensitivity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
these peptides play an important role in the spinal cord for the processing of intense noxious stimuli.
SP and NKA do not appear to be necessary for the development of hypersensitivity, but they may be important in maintaining it.
SP and/or NKAs are not required for the development of hypersensitivity to injury, but that the magnitude of these responses may be reduced.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SP and NKA are not essential for nociception, but are required for the maintenance of the response.
the contribution of SP to the nociceptive transmission is not essential, but that it may be involved in the modulation of nociceptive processing.

SP and/or NKAs are not essential for the transmission of nociceptive information from the periphery to the dorsal horn of the cord, but that they may be involved in modulating the magnitude and duration (i.e., the temporal profile) of nociceptive responses in vivo.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SP and NKA do not appear to be required for nociceptive transmission, but rather prolong nociceptive responses.

SP and NKA are not involved in the development of injury-induced hypersensitivity, but that these neuropeptides may be important for the magnitude and duration, and perhaps the temporal pattern, of behavioral hypersensitivity after nerve injury.
the absence of SP or NKA does not alter the ability of spinal neurons to respond to thermal stimuli.
